title: Security, hosting and POPIA disclosure
subtitle: Okiru ESG Intelligence Platform — vendor due-diligence pack
meta: Prepared for Super Group IT  ·  Version 1.1  ·  17 September 2026
stamp: Okiru ESG Intelligence Platform · Security, hosting and POPIA disclosure · v1.1 · 17 September 2026 · Commercial in confidence
intro: This document describes how the Okiru ESG Intelligence Platform is hosted, how client data is encrypted, which artificial-intelligence services process it and where, how it is backed up, how access is controlled and logged, and how the platform sits against the Protection of Personal Information Act.

It is written for an IT function performing vendor due diligence, so it states what is not in place as plainly as what is. A reader who finds an unlisted weakness is entitled to assume there are others; the open items in section 9 are listed with an owner and a date so they can be assessed rather than discovered.

verification.label: Basis of this disclosure
verification.body: Every statement was read off the running production system — the Azure resource configuration, the Kubernetes cluster, the deployed configuration, the backup store and the source repository. Nothing here is aspirational. Where a control is planned rather than live, it appears in section 9 and nowhere else. Version 1.1 supersedes the 16 September 2026 issue; section 11 lists what changed and why.

sections.title: Where the platform runs, and where the data sits

blocks.text: The platform runs on Microsoft Azure in the South Africa North region (Johannesburg). All primary client data — the operational database, the cache, the document store and the backup store — is created and held in that region.

blocks.text: The platform is a multi-tenant application. Client records are separated logically by organisation, enforced in the application's authorisation layer, rather than by a separate database per client.

sections.title: Which models process client data, and where

blocks.text: The platform uses artificial intelligence in two places: reading uploaded documents (optical character recognition and layout extraction) and interpreting their contents against the ESG and B-BBEE data model. Version 1.0 of this document disclosed that the interpretation service was provisioned in the United States. It has since been moved to South Africa North, and the position is set out precisely below because one part of it is still not fully in-country.

head: Purpose
Service and model
Resource region
Where it is processed
rows: Azure OpenAI, GPT-5 mini class, Global Standard deployment
Any Azure region; data at rest stays in South Africa

blocks.label: The remaining cross-border element, stated exactly
blocks.text: Document reading and embeddings are now entirely within South Africa. Interpretation is not. Microsoft offers the GPT-5 model class in South Africa North only as a Global Standard deployment, which permits inference to be processed in any Azure region; the only in-region alternative is provisioned throughput, which is priced for far larger volumes than ours. What changed is material: the resource, and therefore data at rest, is now in South Africa, and the document text sent for embedding no longer leaves the country. What remains is that prompt content for interpretation may transit another region during inference. That is a transfer under section 72 of POPIA, it is disclosed here rather than left to be found, and closing it is open item 1.

items: Both services are Microsoft first-party Azure services consumed under the Azure enterprise agreement, not third-party AI vendors.
Microsoft does not use Azure OpenAI customer data to train its models, and prompts are not shared with other customers.
No open-weight, self-hosted or consumer AI service processes client data. A key for one third-party inference provider exists in configuration but is empty and no traffic is sent to it.
Extracted figures are always presented for human review before they are scored or published; the platform does not act on a model's output without a person seeing it.
The United States resource that previously served this traffic is retained only as a rollback path and is scheduled for deletion — see open item 1.

sections.title: What is kept, where, and whether it works

head: Aspect
Position
rows: Encrypted managed disk in the cluster, 7-day rolling retention
Copied off-cluster to Azure Blob Storage in the same region, 30-day retention, dated folder per night
The dump publishes a manifest of file sizes; the copy step verifies every uploaded object against it and fails the job on any mismatch
Performed 17 September 2026. Restores the off-cluster copy into an isolated environment; 48 collections and 17,835 documents recovered with no failures
24 hours — backups are nightly. Work done since the last backup is lost
Not yet measured — see open item 4

blocks.label: What the first rehearsal found
blocks.text: The first restore failed. The nightly copy in blob storage was truncated: the step that copied the dump off-cluster ran in parallel with the step that wrote it, so it uploaded files that were still being written. One collection restored 68 of 139 records before the archive ended mid-stream, and every night in the retention window carried the same defect. The copy on the backup disk was always complete; the off-cluster copy — the one that exists for the case where the cluster is gone — had never been restorable. The two steps are now strictly ordered, the dump marks itself complete before anything is copied, and every uploaded object is size-checked against a manifest. The first backup taken after the fix restores completely and reconciles against production collection by collection. This is disclosed rather than quietly corrected because it is the strongest argument available for why a backup nobody has restored should not be counted as a control.

Backups are held in the same Azure region as the production data, which keeps them inside South Africa but means a region-wide failure would affect both. Geo-redundant backup storage is an open item. Rehearsals are now quarterly and recorded.

sections.title: Who can reach the data, and how they prove who they are

head: Control
Position
Status
rows: Email and password; passwords hashed with bcrypt at work factor 12
Email one-time code, required for every account with access to client data
Minimum ten characters, checked against a common-password list that sees through digit substitution, and against the person's own name, email and company
Server-side session store; cookies HTTP-only, secure and same-site restricted; 7-day lifetime; a password reset ends every other session for that user

blocks.text: The firewall runs at a deliberately conservative sensitivity while it is tuned against real traffic: unmistakable attacks are blocked, a single ambiguous match is logged rather than refused. The sensitivity is reviewed monthly and the record of each change is kept with the configuration. A firewall that turns away a client on its first day gets switched off, and then there is no firewall at all.

sections.title: What is recorded when someone acts on client data

blocks.text: The platform writes a unified audit record for security-relevant actions across both application servers. Each entry carries the timestamp, the acting user, the organisation, the action, the resource type and identifier, whether it succeeded or failed, the source IP address, the user agent, the request identifier and the HTTP method and path.

head: Aspect
Position
Status
rows: Sign-in, failed sign-in, lockout, sign-out, second-factor failure, password reset, authorisation decisions, and record creation, change and export
The true client address, taken from the edge and trusted only from the edge's own network ranges
Every record carries a keyed signature over its own contents; each closed day is sealed with a digest, so both alteration and deletion are detectable
Each sealed day is copied to blob storage under a 730-day time-based immutability policy, which prevents alteration or deletion including by us
730 days. Nothing is deleted that has not first been sealed and archived
An organisation administrator can retrieve their own organisation's trail as CSV or JSON, scoped so it cannot be widened to another tenant
A report re-derives each day's digest and compares it with the seal taken at the time
Azure platform logs available; not centralised or retained to a defined policy

blocks.text: The audit trail still lives in the same database as the data it describes, so someone with write access to that database could alter it. What has changed is that they could not do so undetectably: the signature fails on any altered record, and the day's seal fails if a record is removed or inserted. The archived copy is outside their reach entirely.

In POPIA terms Super Group is the responsible party for its own employee and operational data, and Okiru is an operator processing that data on its instruction. The following is our position condition by condition.

Written incident-response and breach-notification plan, with severity levels and a 24-hour client-notification commitment for the most serious. Not yet rehearsed

blocks.label: Operator agreement
blocks.text: Section 21 of POPIA requires a written agreement between a responsible party and its operator obliging the operator to maintain the security safeguards in section 19. We recommend this disclosure be attached to such an agreement rather than standing alone, and we will sign one on Super Group's paper.

sections.title: How Super Group's systems would connect

items: Traffic is HTTPS only, TLS 1.2 or better, to a single named host with a publicly verifiable certificate.
Super Group would allow-list our egress addresses; we would allow-list theirs. Both are static.
Authentication for a system-to-system integration would be a per-client credential with least-privilege scope, rotatable on request and revocable immediately.
We accept data being pushed to us or exposed for us to pull. We do not require access to any Super Group system beyond the agreed endpoint and fields.
An integration endpoint would be exempted from the interactive rate limits and given its own quota, agreed in writing rather than discovered under load.
The field list Super Group's IT function would need to expose is issued separately as an interface specification, derived from the ESG data model rather than from any one company's spreadsheet.

sections.title: What is different from version 1.0, and why

blocks.text: Version 1.0 was issued on 16 September 2026 with twelve open items. This version records what has been closed in the week since. It is included so that a reader can see the direction of travel, and so that any claim that has been strengthened can be checked against the date it changed.

head: v1.0 item
Position now

Partly closed. The service is now in South Africa North; embeddings are processed in-region; interpretation may still transit another region during inference. Restated precisely in section 3
No rate limiting or web application firewall
Closed. Durable per-address limits and per-account lockout across every authentication path, and ModSecurity with the OWASP Core Rule Set in blocking mode at the ingress
Restore never rehearsed; no agreed recovery objectives

Closed for the database. The first rehearsal found that every off-cluster copy was truncated; that is fixed and verified, and recovery objectives are now measured. Full-platform recovery time remains unmeasured as item 4
Closed. Required for every account with access to client data

Closed. Raised to 12, with existing accounts upgraded silently at next sign-in. Password reset previously accepted weaker passwords than sign-up; both now use one policy

Closed. Per-record signatures, daily seals, an append-only archive under a 730-day immutability policy, a 730-day retention policy, and client-retrievable export

Closed. Secret scanning, typecheck, both test suites, dependency audit and container image scanning as merge gates. Known vulnerable dependencies reduced from 127 to 30, with no critical and no unaddressed high
Partly closed. Written, with severity levels, notification timings and a credential-rotation procedure. Not yet rehearsed — item 5

blocks.label: One correction to version 1.0
blocks.text: Version 1.0 stated that there was no rate limiting on authentication endpoints. That was too absolute: a per-address limit did exist on sign-in, but it was held in each process's memory, so it was multiplied by the number of running copies and reset on every deployment, and it covered neither one-time codes nor password reset. The conclusion — that the control could not be relied on — was right; the description was not precise, and it is corrected here.
